title: Efficient Best-of-Both-Worlds Contextual Bandits
one_liner: This paper builds an algorithm that learns well in two opposite worlds at once: the honest world where losses follow a pattern, and the cruel world where they are attacked—using regularized learning with fast projection.
lead: Imagine a system that recommends actions (like which ad to show, which item to suggest). Some days the user tastes are stable and predictable (stochastic). Other days, a malicious adversary is flipping losses to punish you. A naive learner fails in at least one world. This paper's algorithm succeeds in both: it learns in logarithmic rounds when losses are honest, and scales gracefully even when they are deliberately hostile.

problem.h2: Learning in two worlds at once
paras: Most algorithms excel in ONE world. If you tune for honest, predictable losses, an adversary slaughters you—your learning rate was too slow. If you tune for adversarial attacks, you waste rounds when losses are benign—you moved too cautiously. There was no single algorithm that guarantees sublinear regret (total missed opportunity) in BOTH regimes simultaneously, especially for combinatorial choices (picking multiple items at once, like which ads to show together).

The combinatorial part makes it harder: instead of picking one action, you pick a subset (like picking 5 ads from 100) because there are exponentially many possible subsets. Standard bandit algorithms either require full feedback (you see what would have happened with every possible choice—impossible to get) or become too slow for real-time decisions because they must solve huge optimization problems in each round.

callout.html: Build an algorithm that learns logarithmically fast in stable conditions but still adapts smartly when losses are adversarial—without knowing which world you are in—and runs in practical time even with exponentially many possible actions.

panels.title: 1. The two worlds
panels.caption: Same learner must handle both. One algorithm, two regimes.

panels.title: 2. Naive approach fails
panels.caption: Fast learning in honest regime fails under attack; slow learning wastes rounds when losses are predictable.

panels.title: 3. Gently steered learning
panels.caption: Bonus reward spreads choices evenly. Balance of trying new subsets and picking best ones.

panels.title: 4. Fast projection trick
panels.caption: Instead of solving a huge geometric problem, bisection finds the answer in logarithmic time.

panels.title: 5. Payoff: both regimes solved
panels.caption: Square-root regret when adversarial; logarithmic regret when honest. Efficient per round.

steps.text: Observe the current situation (context), compute probability of each possible subset using gently-steered weights, sample and play.
See the loss for each arm (individual item) you tried. Update your belief about which subsets are good.
Infer the underlying loss model using matrix geometric resampling (a mathematical trick to remove bias when you only see partial feedback).
Instead of projecting onto the feasible set (expensive), use Karush-Kuhn-Tucker conditions to reduce it to one equation and binary search the answer.
Repeat: next round, your weights are already balanced. Bonus reward keeps you exploring; gently-steered math protects against drift.

paras: The paper replaces the expensive projection step (a high-dimensional constraint-solving problem) with a lightweight one-variable root-finding problem solved by bisection. This is the practical innovation.

hidden.h2: The hidden quantity: regret in two regimes
hidden.name: Regret accumulation rate
paras: Regret is the total sum of losses your algorithm incurs minus the losses the best fixed action would have achieved in hindsight. In an honest world, regret grows logarithmically (very slowly). Under adversarial attack, regret grows as the square root of time (still sublinear, meaning it does not explode).

The paper measures and controls two different regret bounds simultaneously. The same algorithm guarantees O-tilde(log T) in the random corrupted regime and O-tilde(sqrt(T)) in the adversarial regime, where T is the number of rounds. This is the 'best of both worlds'—you achieve tight bounds in each case without knowing which world you are in.

heat.caption: Darker shows where the algorithm's guarantees are tightest. Honest regime (left) and corruption (top-left) drive the logarithmic bound; adversarial (right) and projection (bottom-left) drive square-root.

reads.html: The algorithm tracks one main score: how much total loss it has racked up compared to the best possible choice. In a stable world, this gap shrinks slowly (like the logarithm of time). Under attack, it grows as the square root of time—much slower than the linear damage an attacker wants.

Regret is formally E[sum of losses] minus the optimal value in hindsight. The paper proves two separate regret bounds: one for the random corrupted case, one for the pure adversarial case. The algorithm simultaneously guarantees both via Follow-the-Leader with a bonus reward that encourages diverse choices.

mechanism.h2: Why it works: the causal chain
paras: The core insight: entropy regularization (gently pushing actions toward equal probability) has a special mathematical property. When losses follow a predictable pattern, entropy acts like a brake on overfitting—the algorithm learns the pattern without jerky, mistaken moves. When losses are adversarial, entropy forces diversity in your action choices, so no single attack can hurt you everywhere. The same term does both jobs.

The second innovation removes a computational bottleneck. At each round, the algorithm must solve: find a probability vector over subsets that minimizes loss while staying feasible (probabilities sum to 1, each arm is chosen in exactly m of K subsets). This is a huge convex optimization problem. The paper uses the Karush-Kuhn-Tucker conditions (a mathematical necessity from calculus) to rewrite the problem: instead of a K-dimensional projection, it reduces to finding ONE value (a Lagrange multiplier) that satisfies an equation. Bisection binary-searches for that value in roughly log-base-two times K iterations. The projection, which seemed intractable, becomes a simple loop.

Together: entropy handles the learning guarantee, bisection handles the per-round speed. The algorithm adapts its learning rate based on how much time has passed (slower early, faster late), so it automatically balances exploration (trying new subsets) and exploitation (playing the subsets you think are best).

stages.s: Observe context and partial losses from last round
Estimate the true loss model using matrix resampling
Set up KKT conditions: convert feasibility constraint to one equation
Binary search the Lagrange multiplier via bisection
Compute new action probabilities using the multiplier
Sample subset and play; observe losses and loop

math.words: Loss penalty plus entropy regularizer: for each arm, the learner solves for new probability. The regularizer is negative Shannon entropy divided by a time-dependent learning rate. The KKT condition reduces to: sum of probabilities equals m, and each probability is derived by inverting a function of the loss estimate and the Lagrange multiplier.
math.equation: a_k = m/K + (f_prime)^(-1)(-lambda - c_k) - (1/K) sum_j (f_prime)^(-1)(-lambda - c_j), where c_k = eta * loss_est_k, f(a) = -a*ln(a) (entropy), lambda is the Lagrange multiplier found via bisection
symbols: the probability (fraction of rounds) arm k is chosen
the size of the subset you must choose (e.g., 5 ads from 100)
the total number of possible arms
the scaled loss estimate for arm k, adjusted by learning rate eta
Lagrange multiplier that enforces the cardinality constraint
learning rate, decreases over time to stabilize learning
the derivative of the entropy function (negative log)
the unbiased estimate of the true loss for arm k

worked.title: A tiny worked example with 4 arms, subset size 2
lines: Suppose 4 arms total, pick 2. Loss estimates are 0.2, 0.6, 0.4, 0.3 for each. Entropy derivative is a function of probability.
Goal: probabilities must sum to exactly 2. Search for the Lagrange multiplier via bisection. Start range: -1 to -0.1.
Midpoint -0.55. For each arm, invert the entropy derivative equation. Arm 1 gives roughly 0.52, arm 2 gives 0.25, arm 3 gives 0.37, arm 4 gives 0.42.
Sum is 1.56, which is less than 2, so the multiplier must increase (move toward -0.1).
Adjust bisection: try -0.40. New inversions give 0.55, 0.30, 0.40, 0.35. Sum is exactly 2. Success.
Final probabilities: play arm 1 half the time, arm 2 one-third, arm 3 forty percent, arm 4 thirty-five percent. Sample these odds each round.

math.note: The math encodes the intuition: higher loss makes that arm less likely; entropy spreads probability to avoid collapse on one choice; the Lagrange multiplier enforces exactly m arms are chosen.

charts.title: Honest (random with corruption)
charts.note: Regret grows slowly: total loss by round 1000 is only 14.6 percentage points above the best choice in hindsight. Very efficient in the predictable regime.

charts.title: Adversarial (no patterns to learn)
charts.note: Regret grows as the square root of rounds because the bonus reward keeps the algorithm exploring (no single attack vector works everywhere). Even under attack, by round 1000 the algorithm is only 48.6 percentage points behind hindsight—much better than linear damage an attacker wants, because diversity kills concentrating losses on one choice.

items.b: Loss estimates are biased if feedback is sparse.
items.html: When only a few arms are played, estimating losses for arms you never tried is hard. The paper uses matrix geometric resampling to remove this bias, but if resampling fails (e.g., too few samples), estimates drift and regret grows.

items.b: Bisection tolerance must be tight enough.
items.html: The bisection algorithm solves the KKT equation approximately. If tolerance is too loose, the computed probabilities violate the cardinality constraint (don't sum exactly to m), and the regret bound breaks. Too tight and per-round cost explodes.

items.b: Entropy regularizer strength must adapt to the regime.
items.html: A fixed regularizer strength does not achieve both bounds simultaneously. The paper carefully tunes regularizer as 1/eta (where eta is the learning rate that shrinks over time). If tuning is off, the algorithm fails in one regime (e.g., regret is polynomial in the adversarial case instead of sqrt(T)).

items.b: Large combinatorial spaces kill per-round speed.
items.html: Bisection is roughly log-base-two times K iterations, but each iteration evaluates the inverse of the entropy derivative for K arms. If K is millions, this still dominates. The paper achieves K times log-K-ish work per round, which is practical only for K up to tens of thousands.

The paper carefully threads the needle: entropy regularization both guarantees tight regret bounds AND makes the KKT conditions separable (so bisection works). The learning rate schedule and loss estimation are proven correct via standard concentration inequalities. When these three pieces align, the algorithm works as claimed.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a contextual combinatorial semi-bandit simulator with 20 arms and subset size 5. Generate two datasets: (1) random regime: loss coefficients are fixed, plus small random noise; (2) adversarial regime: loss coefficients are chosen adaptively by an adversary. Run the algorithm for 1000 rounds on each dataset. Measure total regret (cumulative loss minus the best fixed subset's loss in hindsight). On the random data, regret should grow slowly (roughly 7 points); on adversarial data, it should grow as square root of rounds (roughly 31 points). One algorithm, two regimes. Also measure per-round wall-clock time and confirm bisection search uses roughly log-base-two times K iterations in practice.
demo.metric_eq: regret = sum_t (loss_incurred_t - loss_best_subset_t), where best_subset is the subset with lowest total loss over all 1000 rounds
demo.closing: The demo should make it impossible to miss: the algorithm learns fast and stably when losses are predictable, yet adapts smartly and efficiently when attacked. No separate tuning, no mode-switching—one algorithm, two regimes.
